whisper.text:
Hello everyone, this is Frank DeFreitas and welcome to Holotalk, the Internet's laser and holography talk show, enjoyed in over 42 countries throughout the world. And now, here's this week's show. Michael Harrison. Good morning, Michael. It's Frank DeFreitas. Hi, Frank. How are you doing? Doing good. How are you? Good. You're a busy guy. Yeah. It's been a really busy week. We're getting ready for a trade show that starts on Monday here at work, so I've been working on a demo that's going to be in our main theater, in our booth. Yeah. Well, you know, I have a lot of notes here. I usually try and get as many notes as possible, but for you, I've got your webpage, your blog, you've got a laser info page, you've got your store, you've got your workshops. Rarely are there that many people who are involved with that many aspects of holography anymore. Usually somebody makes holograms. Yeah. Yeah. And... Yeah. It's a little frustrating. The last few months, I've had very little time to actually make a hologram. Yeah. You do absolutely beautiful work. Well, thank you. There's a certain look that holograms have when they're done carefully and properly. It's just an overall look to the hologram, this optical quality. And the holograms that I've seen you create in your home studio, the quality rivals that of those that I've seen on display at the Museum of Holography in New York. And the holograms are just Well, it's not perfect, but I do take a lot of care in the way I go about creating the hologram. There are still elements that I look at and say, well, I wish I'd done that better. Oh, absolutely. That's all the time. Over the last several years. Are you ever 100% happy with a hologram? Sometimes. Sometimes. I mean, there are always things that I'd like to try. But usually when it goes off from beginning to end, I'm usually pretty happy with the end result, or I keep working on it. But, yeah, there are always things that I'd like to maybe do a little different, not necessarily because it was bad or wrong. I'd like to try something new. Maybe on the creative end. Yeah. Yeah. Let me ask you a question. I saw a while back you did that two-color hologram with the flag and the fireworks. Uh-huh. Is that two separate holograms that are just sandwiched together, or did you actually do that on a single plate with the triathlone technique? The latter. And, actually, I definitely credit Lon Moore for exposing. It was really showing me what you can do with that sort of thing. And it was only recently that I was able to give that a shot. It's very labor-intensive, but definitely worth it. That's my favorite type of holography to do is that multiple-color work. Yeah, and it's really striking. I'm kind of surprised myself at how striking it is, especially when you've got two wildly diverging colors, like a bright red and a bright green. Yeah. It just seems to make both of them pop out more than they do in a single color. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. I have always liked to teeter-totter on both edges of the spectrum, where I try to get as far into the deep blue and violet as I can before it goes invisible, and also take it to the point where I try and get as far into the deep red and infrared as possible before it goes invisible to the eye, and then have all of those colors present in the hologram. And it's interesting because if you play your cards right, you can get deeper reds than the 633. Yeah. You can. Yeah. I haven't done that on purpose. Yeah. I've done that on accident a few times. And I definitely would like to have the time to just be able to spend a few days in the lab playing around with different ways of swelling and shrinking just to see what happens. With all that you've done, is this combining this with a full-time career that you have somewhere else and you do your holography in the evenings and weekends when you have time? Actually, mostly I do the holography early, early in the morning. Oh, really? My wife, Susan, thinks I'm somewhat insane for getting up at around 4 a.m. Yeah. Well, there's guys that do squats with 300 and some pounds at 4 a.m., so. Yeah, and I think they're crazy. Yeah. So I guess it all evens out in the end. Yeah, I do have a full-time job. I'm a software developer working in graphics, so it's related in the visual sense to holography. Yeah. And I'm also working on combining some of the graphics work I do during the day, with holography. Unfortunately, I haven't been able to progress with that as fast as I'd like. Mm-hmm. That's one reason I haven't had too much time over the last few months to work on holography is because the job that actually pays most of my bills. Which has to come first, absolutely. Oh, yeah. Why don't we start off with a list here? I don't like to make it as formal as checking items off on the list, but since we're five minutes into the interview, I thought it would be a good idea to start right off with your store.

I don't like to make it as formal as checking items off on the list, but since we're five minutes into the interview, I thought it would be a good idea to start right off with your store. Okay. I go around and visit people's sites. I can't visit their houses, so I have to visit their sites. Yeah. And I was shocked to see what a nice job you did with this store. It's beautiful. Well, thank you. I can't take full credit because I am using an open-source shopping cart called Zen Cart. Yeah. So a lot of the basic layout was taken care of for me, although I have taken great care in taking photographs and putting the basic content in. I don't have very good luck taking photos of holograms. It's taken a lot of trial and error, tips from people on the forum and tips that have been in books and whatnot, and then just trying to work out my own process. Mm-hmm. I found, interestingly enough, the highest-priced digital camera you can buy is not always the best one to use when you're taking a photograph of a hologram. That's interesting. I've got one from several years back that's a fairly cheap Kodak. It wasn't too cheap at the time, but you can buy it cheap now. It actually takes better pictures of holograms than the other cameras I have. Isn't that interesting? Yeah. Maybe because the resolution's not so high. The resolution is probably two megapixel on the camera. Yeah. That's not one of those early Kodak DC-20s, is it? Yeah. Oh, is it? Do you have one of those? Yeah. I have one of those, too. That was Kodak's first digital, wasn't it? Or one of the very early ones? Oh, no. It's not the DC-20. It is one of the DC line. I think the DC-20 was a really old one. Yeah, because I think you could take four high-res pictures with it. Yeah. Yeah. I do have one of those. Do you? That was expensive at the time. It was. Oh, my goodness. And you could take four high-res, I think, like eight low-res pictures with it. Yeah. That's crazy. Yeah. I'm using a slightly newer one, but it was one of the DC line. So you offer your own holograms for sale, and I thought this would be the perfect time, you know, as they say, tis the season, to put the show up. I imagine most people who are involved with holography are probably already aware that you have the store there, but I imagine maybe there are some listeners who do not know, and they may be looking for a hologram to give as a gift to someone special, and they could go over there. And not just get a mass-produced hologram, but a hologram done by a craftsperson that is creating these holograms by hand, one by one. That's true. Each one is made when the order is received. It's very rare that I have extras that I make, just because I don't really like to store them. Mm-hmm. I prefer to make them as somebody requests it. So, yeah, most of these are unique. There will be, you know, slight differences. There will be differences between each hologram, because they are, as you say, handmade. I had lunch with Steve Michael last week. Yeah. And he was talking about the new generation of computer-generated and the computer printers, the three-color printers, that's coming onto the marketplace where someone can supply just a 3D data file and have the hologram printed out. Yeah, that's very interesting. And he was sort of like lamenting on what's that going to be for the rest of us now. And to me... I told him that my impression of that is that it makes what we do more valuable, because take a look at furniture. You can run over to a Walmart or a Kmart and buy a cabinet in a box for $99 and come home and put it together with a screwdriver. But what that does is someone who's a craftsperson and a cabinet maker that works with Quality Woods, that actually boosts their value for what they do and the product that they give to the marketplace. I think that's true. And I think for some people, this is a bad thing. But I think overall for the market, it's a good thing. Yeah. Because it will expose more people to higher-quality holograms at a lower price. Mm-hmm. And at the same time, as you say, people who take more care and produce something that could be considered more of a work of art will benefit more in the long run, because so many people don't really know what a hologram is. Oh, still. Yeah, I'm starting the winter presentations. And they just don't know. Yeah. I don't want to give names away or anything, but I was on the phone with someone the other night and making arrangements for an upcoming keynote. Mm-hmm. And the person had asked me how I will be projecting these images out over top of the audience. Yeah. And it's like, well, we need to get on the same page as far as what this is first. And I still don't understand it after all these years. Well, it's kind of funny, because... You know, holograms were very popular in the 80s to late 80s, and then sort of petered out early 90s. And from that point on, the only holograms that most people have seen have been movies and interpretation of what a hologram should be. Yeah.

And from that point on, the only holograms that most people have seen have been movies' interpretation of what a hologram should be rather than what they really are. And it's a little disappointing because some people have that preconceived notion. And when they see an actual hologram, they're like, well, that's neat, but I can't reach my hand through it. Yes. So I think there's some education still to be done. But again, the technology is advancing. So perhaps, hopefully in our lifetime, maybe holograms will be more like what the movies portray them to be. Although I think what we produce now are beautiful in their own right. Oh, absolutely. I don't think that we necessarily need to strive to meet Hollywood's expectations. You've been involved with holography going back to the 80s, haven't you? Off and on. I can't really. I can't claim involvement during that full-time period. There was a bit of a gap where I wasn't making any holograms. Oh. I remember looking at your first hologram that you had on your website. It's a little castle or something. Yeah, that was the first. Was that a kit or something? Was that castle included in a kit or something or no? No, although I think somebody is doing that now. Yeah. I don't remember who's exactly doing that. Some company, yeah. But no, that was one that I just found at a local shop at the time I was making holograms. And that turned out to be a movie. Yeah. That turned out to be the subject that I used for my first transfer. That was an H2. Oh. Made an H1 on the same film size. So many holographers are going, that's not the way you want to do that. But when you're doing it for the first time, whatever works. And it was probably, well, it was the first really bright H2 I'd ever made. And I still have a few copies of it. And they're just as bright, clean now as they were the day I made them. Isn't that something? Yeah, it really is. What processing regimen are you using? What are you using for your holograms? I notice most of them are in that same range of green. Is that due to the processing regimen that you're using? It is. Unless I'm looking for a specific look, I tend to, I guess I tend to choose green. Although a lot of it is just, you know, what color I feel like doing at the moment. Yeah. But the green tends to be the brightest. Mm-hmm. So that tends to be my default. And it is just from TEA swelling. Oh, okay. Good. It's not necessarily the chemo. It's not necessarily any other chemicals or the developer or the bleach. Although some of my early ones, when I say early, my current sort of block of time making holograms from 2003 on, when I got restarted in it, a lot of the color shifting there was due to the bleach that I was using. Mm-hmm. But these days I'm mainly using the JD2 developer. I see. And then I'm using EDTA bleach. Yeah. I'm actually doing that for both the masters and the copies. Okay. Mm-hmm. You have to buy individual chemicals for that EDTA bleach. Is that correct? I do. Yeah. But I've started buying the individual chemicals anyway. Yeah. There's a friend of mine who also got back into holography, Andres Casais, who lives just down the road from me. Oh, okay. So we tend to share chemical buys and whatnot, so it makes purchasing a little bit easier. Yeah. Texas is actually one of the top subscribers to the Holotalk. Oh, that's good. You know, I mean, Pennsylvania's big, because I'm right here. Of course, New York and California, but I think there's maybe 48 or 49 subscribers just in the state of Texas. Wow. You know, which is less than California, New York, and Pennsylvania, but compared to Mississippi, Yeah. which I think has nine or something, Texas. Well, in some ways, in that regard, I wish Texas were smaller, because we're so spread out here that it's difficult to get with other holographers. Yeah. You had snow down there the other day, didn't you? Yeah. It was mostly ice, but yeah, we actually got some frozen precipitation. Yeah, because I know I was out back in shorts and T-shirt when the Weather Channel was showing the snow plows going through Texas. Yeah. We had roads shut down. People here are not used to snow or ice, and so the whole city tends to shut down. Now, if someone wanted to order one of your holograms from your store, it's pretty easy to do. Do you want to just give them a quick step-by-step process if they visit there? Well, there. Actually, a couple of ways you can do it. Probably the easiest way is just to go to the store and browse the different holograms that are available. You can either register through the store like you would many other retailers, eBay and Amazon, although not that large yet, and then you can either pay by PayPal or credit card. I will also do COD orders. Oh, that's interesting. The first two are inconvenient for you for whatever reason. But you're pretty much covering all the bases. Yeah, I'm trying to. I can't at the moment take direct credit card, but most people I think are okay with PayPal. And then there's also one section where you can do a special order.

Yeah, trying to. I can't at the moment take direct credit card, but most people I think are okay with PayPal. And then there's also one section where you can do a special order. There's some that I don't offer on the store for copyright reasons, but it's perfectly okay to do a special order sort of thing. So those can be requested on a case-by-case basis. Okay. And then I don't know if you've also noticed, I do have some of Lon Moore's old Red Bean holograms for sale as well. Are they on photopolymer? They are. Yeah. And I thought it was a shame that they weren't available more widely, so I wanted to see what I could do to help that. Even though he's no longer making holograms, it would be a shame for those to go off the market as well. Yeah, it's a beautiful work, too. Photopolymer's nice. Wish we could still get it. I wish we could do something. Although there are people working on new versions of it. Hopefully that won't get locked up in the security. Yeah, in the security market as well. Yeah. I just had a box of Ultimate Emulsion and the developer and bleach kit sent, so some night soon I'm going to pop that open and see what I can get out of it. Yeah, that's something else I'd like to try as well. Have you worked with that emulsion yet? I haven't yet. It's one of those that's, you know, I haven't tried it yet, and my experimentation time is somewhat limited these days. Yeah, yeah. So I just haven't done it. Unfortunately, it would be really nice if I could just take a month or two off and just spend all day making holograms. Yeah. Do all the experimentation I want to do. Well, Michael, you know, if you think you could go somewhere with what you would get out of taking two months off, it might be a good investment. Look at it as an investment of time, and if you think that on the back end, you know, your return on investment would be something that would be profitable. It might, and I've been looking at ways to turn this into a full-time business. Yeah. Unfortunately, there seem to be more ways to turn it. I've been doing non-profitable business, but I'm still working on it. So we'll see what we can do here. It's a tough field. It is. A lot of it has to do with education. It's difficult to say that something will be profitable if it hasn't been done before in exactly the way you're looking to do it. Yeah. I'm still trying, though. But when you had said that you may be expanding the store to other areas, is that what you had meant back then? Well. I thought that perhaps you had plans of expanding some of your offerings. I do. In holography is limited. I mean, take something just off the top of my head. Cycling or camping. I mean, the catalogs come out with everything that's involved with cycling or everything that's involved with camping. Holography is still pretty limited as far as what could be offered. It is. And I don't want to say too much just because I don't know if it will be successful. But it is. Okay. Okay. Okay. Okay. Okay. Okay. Okay. Okay. Okay. Okay. I can say it's related to some of the new materials that are coming out and the 3D work that I'm doing in my day job. Great. I'm looking forward to see whatever you do. And you have workshops as well, right? I do. Tell us about the workshops, something that I've done for years and years and years. Yeah, and I'm still feeling my way somewhat through how those should be run. But I've had a few now, some local people who have been interested in finding out how to make holograms. Mm-hmm. And basically I offer those in my home. in my studio and in an adjacent room where I basically have a classroom-type atmosphere. I try to spend as much time in the lab as possible since it's the biggest thing that I can offer people coming in off the street, basically. But I do go over optics and the history of both lasers and holography and who was involved and the basics of how a hologram is formed in the film and what the laser contributes to it and that sort of thing. Then we move into the lab to talk about the equipment, how it's used and lab safety, and then get down to the business of making a hologram. Actually making one. Make a single beam most likely, I would guess? Yeah. Then for later, if somebody wants to come back and sort of continue the workshop, then we can move on to a transfer, that sort of thing. Yep. Well, if anyone writes about... If anyone writes about workshops and I find they're from Texas, I'm going to pass them right over to you. Oh, well, thank you. So that they can take care of that with you there. They're willing to drive. There aren't many... I'm surprised that there aren't many people who actually do holograms that offer workshops. Well, it does take a lot of time, and I find that even though you're trying to schedule things, you really have to tailor it, or at least I feel I have to tailor it to the individual student. Yes, exactly. Yeah. Yeah. And so sometimes... Sometimes it takes a little longer than others, or you never quite know exactly how the workshop is going to go, so there's a little bit of flexibility. And it does take some time to prepare, and then you've got the time for the workshop itself. Yeah. So there is a pretty decent investment in time.

So there's a little bit of flexibility. And it does take some time to prepare, and then you've got the time for the workshop itself. So there is a pretty decent investment in time. I think a lot of the people who are involved in holography, at least that I'm familiar with, are either involved in academic sense, where it's kind of a day job for them. They go in, they do research, and then they have, quote, real life afterwards. And then some people are the tinkers, and I mean that in a good way, where they want to go in and they want to experiment. They want to find out how things work. They're not really necessarily in it to produce the imagery, although that's of course the end result. It's more they're into finding out how the things work at a lower level. And then you have the people who are more interested in final imagery. I think I tend to fall more into that camp. I'm... I describe myself as a tool user. I see. Although I'm capable of making tools, I'd much rather use a tool. Mm-hmm. So I much prefer it when things just work, and I can go in and use the tool to create something else. Yes. That's sort of where I lie in the spectrum. It's sort of straddling the tool maker fence, but more on the tool user side. Mm-hmm. What part of Texas is Plano located in? Is it... It's just north of Dallas. Oh, is it? Yeah. We're actually in Collin County, which is north of Dallas. We're not... Technically, we're not part of Dallas, although it's usually easier to say we're near Dallas. Yeah. Because people know where that is. Born and raised? Yeah, I was actually born in Houston. Oh, okay. And more or less raised up here. My parents moved up here when I was eight years old. Okay. And I'm not saying anything bad about Houston, but I'm glad they moved. Oh, okay. It's just too hot and humid down there. Oh, okay. And I thought that when I was eight. And it's different up by Dallas, huh? Yeah. It is. It tends to be a little cooler and somewhat drier, although the summers can be beastly hot no matter where you are in Texas. We tend to average in the 90s. I've always wanted to visit Dealey Plaza. You know, to be honest, I've never even been there. No kidding. Yeah. That's the first place I'd head if I ever had anything to do in Dallas. I'd be over there right away. And I guess that's part of the problem with living here is I want to go other places. Yeah. So I don't get much time to really tour. Dallas itself, although there are a lot of different places you can go as a tourist, just somebody traveling through the area if you want to see a few sites like Dealey Plaza. Yeah. I definitely recommend Fort Worth as well. There's several places you can go there. Years ago, I was going to do a stereogram of the Zapruder film centered around frame 313. Uh-huh. And was talking to different groups, you know, on the web back then. And it was Usenet, you know, with the groups and things. Uh-huh. Well, I can't tell you the emails and things that I would start to get. It's an interesting topic and an interesting part of history, but there are a lot of nutcases involved with people who follow that. Let me tell you, it was scary. It was scary. And it was like, you know what, I'll move on to something else and maybe revisit this at another time. Yeah. I think I can imagine what that must have been like. Yeah. Yeah. Occasionally, I'll listen to late-night talk radio, and that's where all the nutcases seem to lie. Yeah. Yeah. So, you also have a late... I'm just moving on. I hate to be choppy about things. Oh, that's fine. A laser info page. And this is sort of like, I guess, a daily blog, or maybe not daily, but several times a week, where you post all the information about industry happenings with lasers. Yeah. It's, of course, you know, being in holography, it's something I'm interested in. And I thought... Nobody else is doing this, so I'll try it. And I tend to limit it to information that's specific to either laser use or laser production, and leave the holography sorts of news items to the holography forum. But, yeah, I do... I try to troll the web as frequently as possible and find news items that other people haven't reported about yet. Either news that's... Brand new or just... At least that I find interesting. Yeah. I was on there, and I saw that the highest power pulse from a laser was just achieved recently, and I never knew that until I went to your page. Yeah. And it's not something a lot of people would necessarily go out and wonder about. Yeah. And then there's also, like, the laser line scanning that NOAA has been doing for underwater reefs. And it's kind of... It seems like a simple thing these days, because, you know, you see laser... Laser scanners in a grocery store and that sort of thing. But now they're able to actually take a scanner like that and survey a reef and figure out exactly what's living there. I see. So they're able to track the health of...

scanner like that and survey a reef and figure out exactly what's living there. I see. So they're able to track the health of our planet using lasers. So I think finally, not necessarily this year, but in the last several years, the laser has gone from a solution in search of a problem to a solution solving a plethora of problems. It's really nice to see. Yeah, our reefs are actually undergoing quite a bit of change, and it's very concerning to everyone. And they're able to track it more accurately now. So it won't be, well, there's an error rate of whatever high percentage there used to be. Now they can actually say, yeah, this is the number of animals that were living here last year, and this is how many are living there this year. Yeah. They can either say, well, it's improving or it's not. Yeah, and it's very much holographic in a sense that you can't... have something happen to one life form without having it affect all the other life forms. Very much like a hologram. That's true. You know, and... Like waves moving out from the... Yes, exactly. Your involvement with the Holography Forum, Colin's Holography Forum, I would almost consider you like a co-founder, I guess, in a sense. You've been there since day one and have done so much work. Maybe you'd like to tell folks a little bit about that, but I can't imagine that many people. I mean, you're not even knowing about it. Boy, I would hope not. I can't imagine that if you're interested in holography, you haven't heard about it. Yeah. Yeah. Colin started that forum, I think it was early 2003. It might have been late 2002. And I happened upon the original forum that Christmas, thanks to my wife Susan, and actually you, when she bought me your laser kit. Okay. I got back into holography. I thought, well, okay, I'll check the Internet. I'll check the Internet and see if there's a resource out there. And there was a gold mine of information with the beginnings of the Holography Forum. Got deeply involved. Colin is a great help to everybody I know. He's wonderful to talk to, and it's great that he's kept the forum going. But it's also been wonderful to help as much as I can. There are a lot of great people on the forum. Thank you. I wish there were more people participating. This is something you'll hear on the forum kind of frequently. That happens with all forums. It does. There tends to be more lurkers than there are actual participants. There's a forum that I belong to where there's over 100,000 members of the forum. And depending on what thread you go on and what section you go on, it really is just a handful of people that you see posting all the time. Yeah, you tend to see the same places. Where's the other 99,000 people? Yeah. And you'll go on. And it'll say that there's... You know, 100 people online or something. Oh, there's thousands sometimes in this one particular forum that I follow. And the same people posting, though. So that's the way it happens, though. They're all there. You know, everyone's coming and visiting. And they come and go. But it would be good to participate. Yeah. And some people prefer to watch either because they feel they don't have anything to contribute or there are other people. My own participation over the last couple of months probably hasn't been as active as in previous months. It's partly because other people are sort of filling the gaps. And I think there are enough people on the forum that if somebody doesn't answer a question within a few hours, then probably nobody has a convenient answer. So it's really easy to keep the discussions going. Lately, it's been frequently about red-sensitive DCG. That seems to be what's exciting a lot of people on the forum these days. I just spoke to Dave Batten early this morning to do a show. He'll be on. Your show's going to go up first, so we have enough time during the December holiday season for you. And then probably mid-December, Dave's going to come on and talk about his DCG work. Oh, great. Yeah. So I finished up with him this morning. Yeah, that's another area. I mean, there's so many things that you can do with holography, whether you're focusing on a particular photosensitive medium. Or you're looking at different lasers. Or whatever you are interested in, you could keep yourself busy 24 hours a day playing with different areas of holography. It's definitely interesting to look at what people are doing on the forum. Mm-hmm. That feeling. Well, Michael, is there anything that you'd like to add to the interview that we didn't talk about? I imagine in the future I'll definitely have you on again, but if there's anything this time around. Mm-hmm. Anything for folks in the future, because next summer, next fall, two years from now, three years from now, someone may be listening to this. Well, I guess two things, maybe. One is if you haven't visited the forum lately, go and check it out. Um.

now someone may be listening to this well i guess two things maybe one is if you haven't visited the forum lately go and check it out there's a lot of great resources there and even if you're new to holography and don't feel like you i don't know have gotten enough experience to contribute you can contribute just by asking questions or posting information that you know that maybe isn't already there the other thing is uh one thing i think to watch for the near future probably the next year or two is the full color holography that's coming out as you mentioned earlier the holoprinters i think those are probably going to take at least the advertising world by storm and i think more people will be exposed to what holography is capable of so i think more and more people will start out as they go they're going to go they're going to go they're going to go they're going to go asking, you know, so what else can they do? And I think that's a good opportunity for all the holographers in the world to stand up and say, well, I'll tell you. Mm-hmm. All right. It's still an interesting and very exciting field. I don't see that changing. I have to agree with you. I hope I live long enough to see it come close to its potential. I do as well. Time's running out. Yeah. Hopefully not too soon. Not too soon. I hope not. Anything else? No, I think that's all for now. Okay. Thanks for having me on. I really enjoy having you on, and I know people are going to be thrilled to be able to just click their mouse and hear you speak anywhere in the world. So thank you very much for taking the time. I know you're busy. Well, it was no trouble at all. All right. I really appreciate it. And this will probably, I'd like to have this up probably Sunday night by midnight so that I can get the email blast out. Okay. I'm a little hesitant to send email blasts out over the weekend. I'm a little hesitant to send email blasts out over the weekend. I'm a little hesitant to send email blasts out over the weekend. Right now, because someone may get a notice on a Saturday morning, and by the time these busy weekends are over, they've forgotten to listen on Monday when they would have time or whatever. Yeah. Sort of normal start to the week. Yeah. Get it to them, and then maybe sometime. I know a lot of people listen to this during work, too, because I've been told that. Sometimes it's easier during work. Yeah. All right, Michael. Thank you very much. Have a great weekend. You too. Okay. Bye. Bye-bye. Thank you.

Hello everyone, this is Frank DeFreitas and welcome to Holotalk, the Internet's laser and holography talk show, enjoyed in over 42 countries throughout the world. And now, here's this week's show. Michael Harrison. Good morning, Michael. It's Frank DeFreitas. Hi, Frank. How are you doing? Doing good. How are you? Good. You're a busy guy. Yeah. It's been a really busy week. We're getting ready for a trade show that starts on Monday here at work, so I've been working on a demo that's going to be in our main theater, in our booth. Yeah. Well, you know, I have a lot of notes here. I usually try and get as many notes as possible, but for you, I've got your webpage, your blog, you've got a laser info page, you've got your store, you've got your workshops. Rarely are there that many people who are involved with that many aspects of holography anymore. Usually somebody makes holograms. Yeah. Yeah. And... Yeah. It's a little frustrating. The last few months, I've had very little time to actually make a hologram. Yeah. You do absolutely beautiful work. Well, thank you. There's a certain look that holograms have when they're done carefully and properly. It's just an overall look to the hologram, this optical quality. And the holograms that I've seen you create in your home studio, the quality rivals that of those that I've seen on display at the Museum of Holography in New York. And the holograms are just Well, it's not perfect, but I do take a lot of care in the way I go about creating the hologram. There are still elements that I look at and say, well, I wish I'd done that better. Oh, absolutely. That's all the time. Over the last several years. Are you ever 100% happy with a hologram? Sometimes. Sometimes. I mean, there are always things that I'd like to try. But usually when it goes off from beginning to end, I'm usually pretty happy with the end result, or I keep working on it. But, yeah, there are always things that I'd like to maybe do a little different, not necessarily because it was bad or wrong. I'd like to try something new. Maybe on the creative end. Yeah. Yeah. Let me ask you a question. I saw a while back you did that two-color hologram with the flag and the fireworks. Uh-huh. Is that two separate holograms that are just sandwiched together, or did you actually do that on a single plate with the triathlone technique? The latter. And, actually, I definitely credit Lon Moore for exposing. It was really showing me what you can do with that sort of thing. And it was only recently that I was able to give that a shot. It's very labor-intensive, but definitely worth it. That's my favorite type of holography to do is that multiple-color work. Yeah, and it's really striking. I'm kind of surprised myself at how striking it is, especially when you've got two wildly diverging colors, like a bright red and a bright green. Yeah. It just seems to make both of them pop out more than they do in a single color. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. I have always liked to teeter-totter on both edges of the spectrum, where I try to get as far into the deep blue and violet as I can before it goes invisible, and also take it to the point where I try and get as far into the deep red and infrared as possible before it goes invisible to the eye, and then have all of those colors present in the hologram. And it's interesting because if you play your cards right, you can get deeper reds than the 633. Yeah. You can. Yeah. I haven't done that on purpose. Yeah. I've done that on accident a few times. And I definitely would like to have the time to just be able to spend a few days in the lab playing around with different ways of swelling and shrinking just to see what happens. With all that you've done, is this combining this with a full-time career that you have somewhere else and you do your holography in the evenings and weekends when you have time? Actually, mostly I do the holography early, early in the morning. Oh, really? My wife, Susan, thinks I'm somewhat insane for getting up at around 4 a.m. Yeah. Well, there's guys that do squats with 300 and some pounds at 4 a.m., so. Yeah, and I think they're crazy. Yeah. So I guess it all evens out in the end. Yeah, I do have a full-time job. I'm a software developer working in graphics, so it's related in the visual sense to holography. Yeah. And I'm also working on combining some of the graphics work I do during the day, with holography. Unfortunately, I haven't been able to progress with that as fast as I'd like. Mm-hmm. That's one reason I haven't had too much time over the last few months to work on holography is because the job that actually pays most of my bills. Which has to come first, absolutely. Oh, yeah. Why don't we start off with a list here? I don't like to make it as formal as checking items off on the list, but since we're five minutes into the interview, I thought it would be a good idea to start right off with your store.

I don't like to make it as formal as checking items off on the list, but since we're five minutes into the interview, I thought it would be a good idea to start right off with your store. Okay. I go around and visit people's sites. I can't visit their houses, so I have to visit their sites. Yeah. And I was shocked to see what a nice job you did with this store. It's beautiful. Well, thank you. I can't take full credit because I am using an open-source shopping cart called Zen Cart. Yeah. So a lot of the basic layout was taken care of for me, although I have taken great care in taking photographs and putting the basic content in. I don't have very good luck taking photos of holograms. It's taken a lot of trial and error, tips from people on the forum and tips that have been in books and whatnot, and then just trying to work out my own process. Mm-hmm. I found, interestingly enough, the highest-priced digital camera you can buy is not always the best one to use when you're taking a photograph of a hologram. That's interesting. I've got one from several years back that's a fairly cheap Kodak. It wasn't too cheap at the time, but you can buy it cheap now. It actually takes better pictures of holograms than the other cameras I have. Isn't that interesting? Yeah. Maybe because the resolution's not so high. The resolution is probably two megapixel on the camera. Yeah. That's not one of those early Kodak DC-20s, is it? Yeah. Oh, is it? Do you have one of those? Yeah. I have one of those, too. That was Kodak's first digital, wasn't it? Or one of the very early ones? Oh, no. It's not the DC-20. It is one of the DC line. I think the DC-20 was a really old one. Yeah, because I think you could take four high-res pictures with it. Yeah. Yeah. I do have one of those. Do you? That was expensive at the time. It was. Oh, my goodness. And you could take four high-res, I think, like eight low-res pictures with it. Yeah. That's crazy. Yeah. I'm using a slightly newer one, but it was one of the DC line. So you offer your own holograms for sale, and I thought this would be the perfect time, you know, as they say, tis the season, to put the show up. I imagine most people who are involved with holography are probably already aware that you have the store there, but I imagine maybe there are some listeners who do not know, and they may be looking for a hologram to give as a gift to someone special, and they could go over there. And not just get a mass-produced hologram, but a hologram done by a craftsperson that is creating these holograms by hand, one by one. That's true. Each one is made when the order is received. It's very rare that I have extras that I make, just because I don't really like to store them. Mm-hmm. I prefer to make them as somebody requests it. So, yeah, most of these are unique. There will be, you know, slight differences. There will be differences between each hologram, because they are, as you say, handmade. I had lunch with Steve Michael last week. Yeah. And he was talking about the new generation of computer-generated and the computer printers, the three-color printers, that's coming onto the marketplace where someone can supply just a 3D data file and have the hologram printed out. Yeah, that's very interesting. And he was sort of like lamenting on what's that going to be for the rest of us now. And to me... I told him that my impression of that is that it makes what we do more valuable, because take a look at furniture. You can run over to a Walmart or a Kmart and buy a cabinet in a box for $99 and come home and put it together with a screwdriver. But what that does is someone who's a craftsperson and a cabinet maker that works with Quality Woods, that actually boosts their value for what they do and the product that they give to the marketplace. I think that's true. And I think for some people, this is a bad thing. But I think overall for the market, it's a good thing. Yeah. Because it will expose more people to higher-quality holograms at a lower price. Mm-hmm. And at the same time, as you say, people who take more care and produce something that could be considered more of a work of art will benefit more in the long run, because so many people don't really know what a hologram is. Oh, still. Yeah, I'm starting the winter presentations. And they just don't know. Yeah. I don't want to give names away or anything, but I was on the phone with someone the other night and making arrangements for an upcoming keynote. Mm-hmm. And the person had asked me how I will be projecting these images out over top of the audience. Yeah. And it's like, well, we need to get on the same page as far as what this is first. And I still don't understand it after all these years. Well, it's kind of funny, because... You know, holograms were very popular in the 80s to late 80s, and then sort of petered out early 90s. And from that point on, the only holograms that most people have seen have been movies and interpretation of what a hologram should be. Yeah.

And from that point on, the only holograms that most people have seen have been movies' interpretation of what a hologram should be rather than what they really are. And it's a little disappointing because some people have that preconceived notion. And when they see an actual hologram, they're like, well, that's neat, but I can't reach my hand through it. Yes. So I think there's some education still to be done. But again, the technology is advancing. So perhaps, hopefully in our lifetime, maybe holograms will be more like what the movies portray them to be. Although I think what we produce now are beautiful in their own right. Oh, absolutely. I don't think that we necessarily need to strive to meet Hollywood's expectations. You've been involved with holography going back to the 80s, haven't you? Off and on. I can't really. I can't claim involvement during that full-time period. There was a bit of a gap where I wasn't making any holograms. Oh. I remember looking at your first hologram that you had on your website. I don't remember who's exactly doing that. Some company, yeah. But no, that was one that I just found at a local shop at the time I was making holograms. And that turned out to be a movie. Yeah. But when you're doing it for the first time, whatever works. And it was probably, well, it was the first really bright H2 I'd ever made. And I still have a few copies of it. I notice most of them are in that same range of green. Is that due to the processing regimen that you're using? It is.
